## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{10}{10}{10}{10}{95}{10}
\end{marginfigure}

_*How does a system maintain a coherent working set when execution history inevitably outgrows the processor's attention span?*_

The context window is the L1 working cache of the Stochastic Computer: whatever is resident in context is immediately available for neural attention, and whatever falls outside is permanently forgotten. As an autonomous agent executes a complex, multi-turn task—reading source files, executing shell commands, analyzing stack traces, and parsing documentation—its execution history expands monotonically. Even as foundation models expand supported context lengths to millions of tokens, physical and architectural realities impose hard limits. Quadratic or chunked attention over massive contexts introduces severe latency penalties, inflates per-step token expenditure, and induces 'attention rot,' where relevant instructions and needle facts degrade amid irrelevant noise. Simply appending raw observations to the prompt guarantees eventual context exhaustion, quadratic cost explosion, and semantic failure. An agent runtime must actively govern its working set: deciding what state must remain pinned, what intermediate reasoning can be discarded, what observations must be compressed, and when long-running context must be summarized. Effective context management requires measuring working-set dynamics, engineering compaction and eviction pipelines, mitigating position-encoding decay, and establishing the two-phase commit protocol that separates ephemeral scratchpad reasoning from durable context state.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Formulate context working-set dynamics across multi-turn trajectories, calculating token growth rates and latency inflation under monotonic history accumulation.
- Analyze the phenomena of attention dilution, 'lost in the middle,' and Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) frequency decay across expansive context lengths.
- Architect lossy and lossless context compaction pipelines, implementing deterministic observation filtering, semantic summarization, and structural deduplication.
- Implement attention-sink preservation and sliding-window eviction policies, identifying when historical tokens can be safely pruned without destabilizing generation.
- Design the Two-Phase Chain-of-Thought (CoT) Commit protocol, separating transient, discardable reasoning tokens from committed, durable context state.
- Evaluate the trade-offs between full-context replay, recursive compaction, and hierarchical working sets on downstream benchmark accuracy and operational token cost.

:::

## The Working Set Analogy {#sec-vol3-working-sets-l1-model}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Concrete Systems Hook:**

  - *Context as Working Memory:* The prompt prefix and historical turns staged in context are what the attention mechanism directly computes over; whatever is omitted from the window is invisible to the next forward pass.
  - *The Cost of Prompt Bloat:* Ingesting massive contexts inflates Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), consumes precious accelerator memory, and degrades reasoning precision.

Consider an autonomous software engineering agent tasked with modifying an authentication middleware across a distributed service repository. Rather than isolating the target subpackages, the runtime reads fifty source files into the prompt, staging 250,000 tokens into context. Under an eight-way tensor-parallel inference deployment on NVIDIA H100 SXM5 accelerators, Time-to-First-Token ($T_{\text{TTFT}}$) scales from 450 milliseconds to over 42 seconds. When generating the refactored middleware, the model attempts to invoke a deprecated cryptographic routine, completely ignoring an explicit interface contract specified at token offset 114,000. Ingesting raw state without eviction does not expand the agent's functional capacity; it degrades execution latency and introduces stochastic failure.

### The Working Set Principle

In virtual memory operating systems, Peter Denning formalized the principle that a program can execute efficiently if and only if its active working set of pages resides in physical memory [@denning1968]. The working set $W(t, \tau)$ defines the collection of memory segments referenced across a sliding observation window $\tau$. When the operating system fails to provision sufficient physical frames to accommodate $W(t, \tau)$, the system enters thrashing. In a thrashing state, the memory bus and storage controller become fully saturated servicing page faults, and useful instruction throughput collapses toward zero.

Microprocessors do not attempt to map entire secondary storage volumes into L1 cache lines. Cache architectures succeed because program execution exhibits strong temporal locality (recently accessed addresses are likely to be accessed again) and spatial locality (nearby addresses will be accessed soon). The hardware cache controller continually evicts dormant cache lines to maintain high hit rates within a fixed transistor and thermal budget.

```
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         CPU MEMORY HIERARCHY                            |
|                                                                         |
|  [ Registers / L1 ] <---> [ L2 / L3 Cache ] <---> [ DRAM ] <---> [ Disk]|
|      < 1 ns                   ~3-10 ns             ~60 ns         ~10 us|
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
                                    |
                                    | Systems Architectural Equivalence
                                    v
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                     STOCHASTIC COMPUTER HIERARCHY                       |
|                                                                         |
|  [ Context Window ] <---> [ Paged KV Cache ] <---> [ Local ] <---> [ Git|
|     (Attention)              (HBM / SRAM)          Store       / Data-  |
|                                                  (Vector DB)     base]  |
|      Prompt Tokens            Prefill State        Embeddings   Storage |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

An agent runtime operating over an expansive environment faces the exact same physical invariant. The context window is not a permanent data repository; it is the L1 working memory of the Stochastic Computer. Whatever is staged in the active context window is directly addressable by the neural attention mechanism during the current forward pass. Whatever falls outside the context window is physically unreachable by the model's self-attention layers. Treating the context window as an append-only transaction log guarantees that the agent's resident state will eventually exceed physical capacity.

### The Memory Hierarchy of the Stochastic Computer

To balance operational latency, retrieval bandwidth, and token expenditure, modern computer systems organize storage into a tiered hierarchy based on latency and cost per byte. The agent runtime reproduces this classic hierarchy, mapped onto neural infrastructure (@tbl-memory-hierarchy-comparison).

| Memory Tier         | Classical System Component          | Stochastic Computer Equivalent                       | Hardware Medium                                  | Typical Access Latency                      | Durability & Access Model                                              |
|:--------------------|:------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **L1 Working Set**  | Processor Registers / L1 Data Cache | Active Context Window (Prompt Tokens)                | Accelerator SRAM / Compute Registers             | Immediate (0 overhead per forward pass)     | Volatile; bounded by maximum sequence length $L_{\text{ctx}}$.         |
| **L2 Acceleration** | L2/L3 Static RAM (SRAM) Cache       | Key-Value (KV) Cache                                 | Accelerator High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM)          | Low (sub-millisecond per token decode step) | Ephemeral; discarded upon session completion or context eviction.      |
| **L3 Operational**  | Main System Memory (DRAM)           | Ephemeral Scratchpad, Session Log, Working Buffers   | Host RAM / Local Key-Value Store (Redis, SQLite) | Moderate (~1 to 10 ms via local RPC)        | Semi-durable; survives across turns, indexed by explicit query keys.   |
| **Secondary Store** | NVMe SSD / Network Attached Storage | Vector Database, Code Repository, External Artifacts | Persistent Block Storage / Cloud Object Store    | High (50 to 500 ms via network I/O)         | Durable; cold storage requiring explicit external retrieval pipelines. |

: Architectural mapping between classical computer storage tiers and the Stochastic Computer memory hierarchy. {#tbl-memory-hierarchy-comparison}

In this hierarchy, the prompt staging area provides zero-latency access during transformer inference, but it incurs the highest operational cost. When an agent copies an entire source tree or database dump into L1 context memory, it commits the systems equivalent of copying an entire hard drive into processor registers.

### Physical Costs of Context Bloat

Ingesting non-working-set tokens incurs severe penalties across three concrete systems dimensions:

1. **Accelerator Memory Footprint ($M_{\text{KV}}$):** Transformer inference requires staging key and value vectors for every token in the active context across every layer of the network. Under Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), the memory footprint of the KV cache is governed by:
   $$M_{\text{KV}} = 2 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{kv\_heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times b \times L_{\text{ctx}}$$
   where $n_{\text{layers}}$ is the layer depth, $n_{\text{kv\_heads}}$ is the number of key-value heads, $d_{\text{head}}$ is the projection dimension, $b$ is the data precision in bytes (such as 2 bytes for FP16/BF16), and $L_{\text{ctx}}$ is the active sequence length. For a 70-billion-parameter model ($n_{\text{layers}} = 80$, $n_{\text{kv\_heads}} = 8$, $d_{\text{head}} = 128$) running at FP16 precision, a 250,000-token context consumes over 81 gigabytes of accelerator memory for the KV cache alone, starving the hardware of batching capacity and driving device memory into out-of-memory (OOM) faults.

2. **Pre-fill Latency Inflation:** During the initial prefill phase of inference, standard dense self-attention computes pairwise inner products across the entire prompt sequence, scaling quadratically with sequence length ($O(L_{\text{ctx}}^2 \cdot d_{\text{model}})$ FLOPs). When an agent loads unnecessary background pages, Time-to-First-Token ($T_{\text{TTFT}}$) increases by orders of magnitude, transforming interactive tool-use loops into batch-processing bottlenecks.
3. **Attention Dilution and Semantic Rot:** Neural attention uses a softmax normalization across the sequence length:
   $$\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$
   As sequence length $L_{\text{ctx}}$ grows with irrelevant tokens, the softmax denominator sums over a massive volume of distractor keys. The probability distribution over relevant tokens flattens, reducing the signal-to-noise ratio. The model experiences attention dilution, increasing the likelihood that it misses critical system instructions, interface definitions, and tool output schemas.

Treating the context window as an unbounded append-only log violates fundamental memory management principles. To maintain execution coherence over long-horizon tasks, the agent runtime must actively govern its working set: pinning invariant directives, evicting stale observations, and caching intermediate state.

Building an effective context management subsystem requires examining the underlying hardware and algorithmic bottlenecks inside the transformer architecture. In @sec-vol3-working-sets-dynamics, we analyze how attention scaling limits, memory-bandwidth saturation, and positional encoding decay establish the physical boundaries of neural working memory.

## Context Scaling Bottlenecks {#sec-vol3-working-sets-physics}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Context Scaling Bottlenecks {#sec-vol3-working-sets-physics}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Transformer self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length ($\mathcal{O}(T^2)$), and attention weights disperse across long token distances, causing severe retrieval degradation ("lost in the middle").
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - An evaluation shows that when a critical security token is placed in the first 10% or last 10% of a 128k prompt, retrieval accuracy is 98%; when placed at 50% depth, accuracy drops to 52%.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *Quadratic Compute and Memory Complexity:* Standard full self-attention requires computing an $N \times N$ attention matrix ($Q K^T / \sqrt{d}$), requiring $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ compute and memory bandwidth during prefill.
  - *Attention Dispersion ("Lost in the Middle"):* Softmax normalization over tens of thousands of tokens flattens probability mass; attention sinks at beginning and end tokens starve middle tokens of representational fidelity.
  - *The Architectural Imperative:* Massive context windows do not eliminate the need for memory management; they make disciplined working set curation essential.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Figure: `@fig-lost-in-the-middle` [insert link here: books/vol3/04_working_sets/images/svg/lost_in_the_middle_rope_decay.svg] (U-shaped retrieval accuracy curve across relative context position).
- **Seminal Literature:**
  - Nelson F. Liu et al. (2024, *Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts*).
- **Causal Bridge to 4.3:** How does this physical dispersion manifest in multi-turn agent trajectories as "context rot"?
-->

### Quadratic Complexity and Memory Bandwidth Limits

The physical scaling limits of the transformer context window originate in the mathematical formulation of self-attention. During the prefill phase, when an agent processes a sequence of $L_{\text{ctx}}$ tokens, the model computes pairwise dot products between all query vectors $Q \in \mathbb{R}^{L_{\text{ctx}} \times d_k}$ and key vectors $K \in \mathbb{R}^{L_{\text{ctx}} \times d_k}$. Across an architecture with $n_{\text{layers}}$ layers and $n_{\text{heads}}$ attention heads per layer, computing the unnormalized attention logits matrix $S = Q K^\top / \sqrt{d_k}$ requires:

$$\text{FLOPs}_{\text{prefill}} = 4 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{heads}} \times d_k \times L_{\text{ctx}}^2 = 4 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times d_{\text{model}} \times L_{\text{ctx}}^2$$

FLOP consumption scales quadratically ($\mathcal{O}(L_{\text{ctx}}^2)$) with prompt length. While tiled computation algorithms such as FlashAttention eliminate the need to materialize the $L_{\text{ctx}} \times L_{\text{ctx}}$ intermediate attention matrix in High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) by fusing softmax reduction into accelerator Static RAM (SRAM), arithmetic intensity remains bounded by sequence length. The total prefill execution latency $T_{\text{prefill}}$ decomposes into linear projection overhead and quadratic attention calculation:

$$T_{\text{prefill}} = \alpha L_{\text{ctx}} + \beta L_{\text{ctx}}^2$$

where $\alpha$ represents memory-bandwidth-bound matrix-vector transfers for token embeddings and feed-forward layers, and $\beta$ captures the compute-bound pairwise attention inner products across all layers. As $L_{\text{ctx}}$ expands from $4\text{,}000$ to $128\text{,}000$ tokens, the quadratic term dominates wall-clock time, converting interactive agent turns into batch-processing delays.

During the subsequent autoregressive decoding phase, where tokens are generated one at a time, each new token query attends to all $L_{\text{ctx}}$ cached key-value pairs. While the computational complexity per step is linear ($\mathcal{O}(L_{\text{ctx}})$), memory bandwidth consumption is severe: the accelerator memory controller must stream the entire active Key-Value (KV) cache from HBM to compute registers for every single generated token. When $L_{\text{ctx}}$ reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens, inference shifts entirely from compute-bound to memory-bandwidth-bound, capping decoding throughput regardless of available tensor-core compute capacity.

### Attention Dispersion and the "Lost in the Middle" Effect

Beyond physical throughput constraints, scaling the context window degrades retrieval fidelity. Standard self-attention normalizes attention scores across sequence length using the softmax operator:

$$A_{i,j} = \frac{\exp\left(\frac{Q_i K_j^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)}{\sum_{m=1}^{L_{\text{ctx}}} \exp\left(\frac{Q_i K_m^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)}$$

As sequence length $L_{\text{ctx}}$ grows by orders of magnitude, the summation in the denominator accumulates probability mass over tens of thousands of background tokens. Even when individual non-relevant tokens produce small unnormalized dot products, their collective sum in the denominator exerts upward pressure on the normalizer, compressing the peak attention probabilities assigned to ground-truth tokens. The resulting distribution suffers from attention dispersion: probability mass flattens over the expanded token horizon, depressing the signal-to-noise ratio of critical facts.

This mathematical dispersion is compounded by structural biases in transformer position encodings and causal masking. As demonstrated by Nelson F. Liu et al. (2024), autoregressive language models exhibit an empirical U-shaped performance curve across context depth, commonly designated the "lost in the middle" phenomenon.

![Retrieval accuracy across relative context depth in long-context models. Precision remains high near the prompt prefix (due to attention sink behavior) and prompt suffix (due to recency bias), but degrades severely across the central 80% of the context window.](images/svg/lost_in_the_middle_rope_decay.svg){#fig-lost-in-the-middle}

In empirical evaluations over a 128,000-token context window ($L_{\text{ctx}} = 131\text{,}072$), model performance varies sharply as a function of target position (@fig-lost-in-the-middle):

- **Prefix Placement (0% to 10% Depth):** When a critical authorization token or schema definition is placed in the initial 10% of the prompt, retrieval accuracy reaches 98.4%. Initial tokens act as structural "attention sinks," accumulating baseline attention weights across all downstream layers regardless of semantic content.
- **Suffix Placement (90% to 100% Depth):** When the target token is placed within the final 10% of the prompt immediately preceding generation, retrieval accuracy reaches 97.9%, driven by recency bias and causal mask locality.
- **Central Placement (40% to 60% Depth):** When the exact same token is positioned at 50% relative depth, retrieval accuracy collapses to 52.1%.

Submerged in the interior of the prompt, the target key vector fails to overcome the accumulated normalization mass of preceding distractors, causing the model to hallucinate default values or overlook explicit constraints.

### The Architectural Imperative for Working-Set Curation

These physical and statistical realities demonstrate that expanding hardware context windows does not solve the memory management problem. A million-token context window provides a larger virtual address space, but it does not guarantee reliable random access across that space.

In classical operating systems, virtual memory abstracts physical DRAM into an expansive 64-bit address space ($2^{64}$ bytes). However, an application that blindly touches pages across its entire virtual address space without maintaining spatial or temporal locality induces page thrashing, spending all its execution cycles servicing page faults at the storage controller.

In the Stochastic Computer, treating the context window as an append-only transaction log induces the neural equivalent of thrashing:

1. **Monotonic Cost Inflation:** Every execution step re-reads and bills for the entire accumulated sequence length. A 30-turn agent trajectory that expands to 100,000 tokens consumes millions of billable tokens on redundant observations, multiplying operational expenditures.
2. **Deterministic Latency Growth:** Time-to-first-token grows quadratically with prompt size, increasing round-trip execution latency and degrading interactive responsiveness.
3. **Representational Degradation:** Critical system instructions pinned at the start of execution remain stable, but intermediate observations and decisions pushed into the middle of the context window become invisible to downstream attention heads.

An agent runtime cannot rely on model scale to compensate for unbounded memory growth. Long-horizon execution requires active working-set curation: algorithms that dynamically evict stale observations, compress historical trajectories, and pin essential state.

How this physical dispersion manifests as operational failure within iterative tool-use trajectories—inducing the progressive failure mode known as "context rot"—is analyzed in @sec-vol3-working-sets-dynamics.

## Context Accumulation Rot {#sec-vol3-working-sets-context-rot}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Context Accumulation Rot {#sec-vol3-working-sets-context-rot}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Repeated multi-turn execution accumulates obsolete tool outputs, failed command traces, and stale observations; this "context rot" acts as an attentional sink that drags down decision accuracy.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - An agent attempting 10 file edits accumulates 40,000 tokens of compiler error logs from earlier failed attempts. By turn 8, the model begins repeating errors it made in turn 2 because the prompt is dominated by failure patterns.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *Mechanisms of Context Rot:* Stale file versions, obsolete variable values, verbose compiler tracebacks, and historical dead ends remaining in context.
  - *Attentional Sinks:* High-frequency error tokens act as gravitational attractors during autoregressive generation, biasing the model to regenerate similar erroneous syntax.
  - *Trajectory Divergence:* As context rot increases, the probability of a catastrophic wrong action compounds, eventually leading to unrecoverable trajectory drift.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Attention heat map showing attention mass concentrating on historical error traces rather than the system goal.
- **Causal Bridge to 4.4:** How should an agent runtime structure and partition the active prompt to prevent context rot?
-->

In an append-only agent execution harness, every observation, tool invocation, and runtime return value is committed irrevocably to the active context buffer. When an autonomous agent executes a long-horizon task across dozens of iterative turns, this unconstrained accumulation introduces *context accumulation rot*: the progressive degradation of decision quality caused by the retention of obsolete, invalid, or distracting execution artifacts in the active Key-Value (KV) cache.

Consider an agent tasked with modifying an unfamiliar software repository. To implement a ten-line change, the runtime executes an iterative loop: reading source files, editing code, invoking a compiler, and inspecting error traces. If each compilation failure produces a 4,000-token diagnostic dump containing verbose stack traces, syntax errors, and environment variables, ten failed attempts deposit 40,000 tokens of dead-end telemetry into the context. By turn 11, the primary system prompt and the current file contents occupy fewer than 3,000 tokens, submerged beneath tens of thousands of tokens of historical failures. The effective signal-to-noise ratio of the working memory:

$$\mathrm{SNR}_{\text{context}} = \frac{L_{\text{signal}}}{L_{\text{signal}} + L_{\text{noise}}}$$

collapses from $0.95$ at initialization to under $0.07$. Context rot is not merely an efficiency bottleneck that inflates prefill latency and billing costs; it is an active corruptor of the model's conditional probability distribution.

### Mechanisms of Contextual Contamination

Context rot manifests through three distinct systems mechanisms within the prompt buffer:

1. **State Invalidation and Inconsistency:** When an agent updates a local resource—such as rewriting a configuration file or altering a database schema—the historical transcript retains both the pre-modification state $v_0$ and the post-modification state $v_1$. Subsequent generation steps require attention heads to resolve entity references across mutually contradictory representations. Because positional encoding models assign high absolute or relative distance to earlier tokens without explicitly invalidating them, self-attention heads frequently bind attributes from stale states, leading the agent to hallucinate variables or paths that were previously discarded.
2. **Telemetry Overhang:** Standard system tooling is designed for human operators, not token-constrained neural processors. Command-line utilities dump verbose stack traces, unresolved linker warnings, and unpaginated directory listings. These unparsed text streams consume substantial fractions of the context budget with low-entropy syntax (delimiters, memory addresses, boilerplate licenses) that provides negligible mutual information regarding the underlying fault.
3. **Hypothesis Bloat:** Intermediate reasoning traces (such as scratchpads and chain-of-thought blocks) frequently explore speculative, incorrect trajectories. When an agent tests an invalid hypothesis (e.g., assuming an API endpoint uses HTTP GET rather than POST), that reasoning remains resident in context. In subsequent steps, the model attends to its own prior reasoning traces, treating past internal rationalizations as established architectural ground truth.

### Error Tokens as Attentional Sinks

Autoregressive language models generate tokens by computing attention distributions conditioned on past context:

$$P(y_t \mid y_{<t}) = \mathrm{Softmax}\left(\frac{Q_t K_{<t}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)$$

Because foundational transformers are trained on web-scale text using next-token prediction, induction heads within the network are strongly optimized for in-context pattern completion. When the context window becomes saturated with thousands of tokens of compilation failures, exception traces, and malformed command syntax, these tokens function as statistical attractors.

![Attention allocation across transformer layers during autoregressive generation in a degraded context. Query tokens from the active decision turn attend overwhelmingly to repetitive compiler tracebacks and superseded code blocks in the middle of the context, starving the initial system prompt and current target state of attention mass.](images/svg/context_rot_attention_map.svg){#fig-context-rot-attention-map}

As illustrated in @fig-context-rot-attention-map, query vectors at step $t$ distribute significant attention mass across the repetitive failure patterns in the middle context. This induces severe generative bias: the model begins sampling tokens that mirror the dominant structural patterns in its history. Rather than synthesizing novel corrective actions, an agent suffering from context rot repeatedly re-executes the exact commands that failed several turns prior, or reintroduces syntax errors that were previously corrected. The historical failure records actively train the in-context distribution to fail.

### Compounding Trajectory Divergence

The operational consequence of context rot is trajectory divergence. Let $p_k$ represent the probability of an agent selecting a valid, progress-making action at step $k$. In an uncontaminated context, $p_k \approx p_0$. Under context rot, $p_k$ degrades as a function of accumulated noise tokens $L_{\text{noise}}$:

$$p_k = p_0 \cdot \exp(-\gamma \cdot L_{\text{noise}})$$

where $\gamma > 0$ represents the empirical noise sensitivity of the underlying foundation model. For a task requiring $N$ sequential correct decisions, the end-to-end trajectory success probability $P_{\text{success}}$ compounds multiplicatively:

$$P_{\text{success}} = \prod_{k=1}^N p_k = p_0^N \exp\left(-\gamma \sum_{k=1}^N L_{\text{noise}, k}\right)$$

When $L_{\text{noise}}$ grows monotonically with each turn, $P_{\text{success}}$ collapses exponentially. Once an agent enters an error loop, each subsequent failure appends additional diagnostic noise, accelerating the rate of decay $\gamma \cdot L_{\text{noise}}$. The system enters an unrecoverable failure spiral: the Trajectory Goodput:

$$G = \frac{\sum T_{\text{success}}}{\sum T_{\text{all}}}$$

drops toward zero, while token and financial expenditures grow quadratically.

Treating the context window as an append-only ledger violates the core systems principle of working-set hygiene. To sustain long-horizon execution, an agent runtime cannot permit tools and environments to write directly to a flat context buffer. The runtime must enforce explicit architectural boundaries between permanent task instructions, durable state variables, and transient execution telemetry. How an agent runtime structures and partitions this context space to isolate operational noise is examined in @sec-vol3-working-sets-partitioning.

## Prompt Layout Architecture {#sec-vol3-working-sets-staging}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Prompt Layout Architecture {#sec-vol3-working-sets-staging}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Prompt layout is a systems memory layout problem; structuring context into an immutable static prefix, a compacted dynamic working body, and an explicit instruction suffix optimizes attention and cache reuse.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - Moving the system goal and strict formatting constraints from the top of a 50k prompt to the very end (suffix) increases schema adherence from 78% to 99%.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *The Three-Zone Memory Layout:*
    1. *Static Prefix (Zone 1):* System prompt, tool schemas, invariant contracts. Immutable across turns, maximizing prefix caching.
    2. *Dynamic Working Body (Zone 2):* Active code snippets, recent observations, episodic retrievals. Actively compacted and pruned.
    3. *Recency & Instruction Suffix (Zone 3):* Immediate task goal, latest observation, output format schema. Positioned at the end of the context to exploit recency attention bias.
  - *Position-Aware Staging:* Ensuring that high-priority constraints never land in the "lost in the middle" dead zone.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Diagram: `@fig-context-staging-layout` showing the three-zone memory architecture.
- **Causal Bridge to 4.5:** When the dynamic working body exceeds token limits, how does the runtime compact it?
-->

In an autonomous agent runtime, prompt assembly is fundamentally a physical memory layout problem. A naive agent implementation treats the context window as a flat, append-only buffer, serializing permanent system invariants, volatile tool outputs, historical command transcripts, and target response schemas into an undifferentiated token stream. This unprincipled memory layout introduces two severe hardware-level failure modes. First, it defeats prefix caching within the inference engine by invalidating the key-value (KV) cache across sequential execution turns. Second, it deposits high-priority behavioral constraints into the attentional dead zone of the transformer, where self-attention heads exhibit minimal sensitivity. Rather than assembling prompts via arbitrary string concatenation, an agent runtime must manage context as structured virtual memory, partitioning the sequence space into distinct functional zones characterized by differing update frequencies, cache lifecycles, and positional priorities.

The necessity of structured prompt staging is dictated by the positional mechanics of the self-attention operator:

$$\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{Softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

In decoder-only autoregressive transformers, empirical attention distributions over long sequence lengths exhibit pronounced U-shaped positional sensitivity, commonly termed the "lost-in-the-middle" effect. Query vectors at the active decoding step concentrate their attention mass disproportionately on two regions: the initial sequence positions (which function as permanent statistical sinks) and the terminal sequence positions (which constitute the immediate causal receptive field). Intermediate tokens—separated by thousands of steps from both the origin and the generation boundary—suffer substantial attentional attenuation. In a benchmark evaluation across a 50,000-token context window, positioning task goals and strict JSON schema formatting constraints exclusively at the beginning of the context buffer (tokens 0 to 500), separated from the generation point by 48,000 tokens of file contents and command telemetry, yields a schema adherence rate of only 78%. Re-staging those identical operational constraints into a terminal instruction suffix immediately preceding the autoregressive generation point elevates schema adherence to 99%. Context positioning directly governs execution fidelity.

### The Three-Zone Context Architecture

To reconcile physical hardware efficiency with attentional fidelity, the agent runtime partitions the prompt buffer into three explicit functional tiers: the Static Prefix ($Z_1$), the Dynamic Working Body ($Z_2$), and the Recency Suffix ($Z_3$), as illustrated in @fig-context-staging-layout.

![The three-zone prompt layout architecture. The immutable static prefix (Zone 1) maximizes KV cache reuse across sequential turns. The dynamic working body (Zone 2) stores volatile execution telemetry and is actively pruned by the runtime. The recency and instruction suffix (Zone 3) occupies the terminal attention receptive field, anchoring schema compliance and the active sub-goal.](images/svg/context_staging_layout.svg){#fig-context-staging-layout}

**Zone 1: The Static Prefix ($Z_1$).** Zone 1 occupies the lowest physical token addresses $[0, L_{Z_1}-1]$. It contains invariant systems declarations: the base system prompt, persona directives, security boundaries, available tool declarations, and typed JSON schemas. The cardinal systems invariant of Zone 1 is absolute immutability: its content must remain byte-for-byte identical across all turns of an agent session. Modern inference engines—such as vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and SGLang—utilize radix trees and page-table memory architectures (such as PagedAttention) to cache the intermediate KV tensors of prefilled sequences. The physical memory footprint of the KV cache across $L$ tokens is:

$$\mathrm{Memory}_{\text{KV}} = 2 \times L \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times b_{\text{bytes}}$$

When Zone 1 is strictly static, the inference engine computes the KV activations for these tokens exactly once on turn 1. On all subsequent turns $t > 1$, the engine matches the prefix hash in its radix cache, completely bypassing the $O(L_{Z_1}^2)$ attention prefill computation and reducing turn latency by hundreds of milliseconds. Inserting dynamic tokens into Zone 1—such as timestamps, turn counters, or ephemeral session identifiers—alters the prefix hash, forces a complete cache miss, and mandates redundant prefill compute on every step. Furthermore, the runtime must pad $L_{Z_1}$ to integer multiples of the engine's physical page allocation (typically 16 or 64 tokens) to align the static-dynamic boundary with physical KV cache pages.

**Zone 2: The Dynamic Working Body ($Z_2$).** Zone 2 occupies the intermediate token range $[L_{Z_1}, L_{Z_1} + L_{Z_2} - 1]$. It serves as the volatile heap of the agent, housing variable-length operational telemetry: file system excerpts, tool execution outputs, compiler tracebacks, git diffs, and episodic search results. Because Zone 2 resides within the attentional trough of the context window, it must never host critical routing instructions or output schemas. Instead, it stores reference telemetry that the model selectively queries during execution. Unlike Zone 1, Zone 2 is non-monotonic and mutable: the runtime actively instruments, truncates, compresses, and reorders its contents. If the runtime permitted Zone 2 to grow without intervention, accumulated tool logs would rapidly saturate the physical context limit $L_{\text{max}}$, starving the model of working space.

**Zone 3: The Recency and Instruction Suffix ($Z_3$).** Zone 3 occupies the terminal token positions $[L - L_{Z_3}, L - 1]$, positioned directly adjacent to the model's autoregressive generation boundary. Zone 3 operates as the active instruction register of the agent architecture, staging three mandatory fields:

1. *The Immediate Sub-Goal:* The specific, granular objective that must be resolved during the current execution step, isolated from the overarching multi-phase task plan.
2. *The Latest Environmental Delta:* The unmasked return code and trimmed payload of the most recent tool invocation, ensuring the agent reacts immediately to ground-truth state changes.
3. *The Output Schema Constraint:* An explicit reinforcement of the expected response serialization (such as a strict JSON schema or tool call syntax), overriding any degenerative patterns present in historical telemetry.

By staging these control tokens within the recency receptive field, the runtime guarantees that the query vectors generated at step $L$ directly cross-attend to their target schemas without undergoing positional dispersion across the intermediate history.

### Position-Aware Staging Invariants

To maintain operational stability across long execution horizons, the context orchestrator enforces strict boundary invariants across the three memory zones. Given a hardware context window $L_{\text{max}}$ and a reserved output generation budget $L_{\text{gen}}$, the dynamic working body budget $L_{Z_2}$ is constrained by:

$$L_{Z_2} \le L_{\text{max}} - \left(L_{Z_1} + L_{Z_3} + L_{\text{gen}}\right)$$

Zone 1 and Zone 3 operate with fixed token reservations ($L_{Z_1}$ pinned at initialization, and $L_{Z_3}$ dynamically budgeted to accommodate the maximum expected single-step tool response and schema payload). When execution begins, Zone 2 claims the entire remaining balance. The context orchestrator continuously monitors the token footprint of incoming tool observations. If a raw observation threatens to violate the upper bound of $L_{Z_2}$, the runtime refuses to append it directly to the context. Permitting an observation to overflow $L_{Z_2}$ would either truncate the critical instruction suffix in Zone 3 or trigger an unrecoverable out-of-memory exception during generation.

While Zone 1 remains permanently pinned in the KV cache and Zone 3 dynamically shifts forward to frame the active decision boundary, Zone 2 inevitably expands as an agent traverses file trees, executes diagnostics, and compiles code. When the volume of raw operational telemetry exhausts the allocation budget $L_{Z_2}$, the runtime cannot simply drop incoming data or allow unconstrained eviction. It must execute deterministic context compaction, selective pruning, and hierarchical summarization to preserve the coherence of its working memory. The engineering of these compaction and eviction pipelines is examined in @sec-vol3-working-sets-compaction.

<!-- SECTION_END: 4.4 -->

<!-- SECTION_START: 4.5 (#sec-vol3-working-sets-compaction) -->
## Lossy Context Compaction {#sec-vol3-working-sets-compaction}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Lossy Context Compaction {#sec-vol3-working-sets-compaction}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Context compaction reduces prompt size while preserving decision-critical information through lossless filtering, AST-guided pruning, and structured entity extraction.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - A test runner outputs 5,000 lines of standard output containing 4,995 passing test names and 5 assertion failures. Compaction strips the passing lines, reducing 80,000 tokens to 400 tokens with zero loss of diagnostic signal.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *Lossless Filtering:* Stripping ANSI terminal codes, repeated whitespace, progress bars, and redundant log lines via deterministic rules before context injection.
  - *Structured Pruning:* Using AST parsers to extract only modified functions or referenced class interfaces, omitting unaffected repository boilerplate.
  - *Semantic Extraction:* Transforming raw text into dense structured records (e.g. converting a 10-page HTML page into a 20-line markdown table of links and headers).
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Table: Compaction ratios and information retention across raw vs. filtered vs. AST-pruned inputs.
- **Causal Bridge to 4.6:** When detailed step histories must be retained over hundreds of turns, how does the runtime maintain long-term coherence?
-->

The dynamic working body ($Z_2$) acts as an unbuffered sink for operational telemetry generated by external tool execution. When an environment emits high-volume diagnostic streams, appending raw byte streams directly into context memory degrades system performance across two physical dimensions. First, it inflates the KV cache footprint linearly with token count, increasing memory bandwidth pressure during decoding. Second, it incurs quadratic prefill attention computation across subsequent turns without increasing the entropy of the decision-making state.

Consider an automated test runner executing across a monorepo. The process emits 5,000 lines of standard output containing 4,995 passing test declarations and 5 assertion failures with stack traces. Injected verbatim, this stream consumes approximately 80,000 tokens—often exceeding the entire dynamic allocation budget $L_{Z_2}$ or forcing the eviction of prior architectural context. However, the agent's decision logic requires only the identity of the failed suites, the assertion conditions, and the line numbers of the faulting frames. By stripping passing indicators and collapsing repetitive tracebacks, the runtime reduces the payload from 80,000 tokens to 400 tokens. This represents a compaction ratio of:

$$R_C = \frac{L_{\text{raw}}}{L_{\text{compact}}} = 200$$

achieved with zero loss of actionable diagnostic signal. Context compaction is the active reduction of prompt volume through three hierarchical tiers: deterministic lossless filtering, syntax-aware structured pruning, and semantic extraction. Each tier trades off computational overhead against compression efficiency, maximizing information density within $L_{Z_2}$.

### Deterministic Lossless Filtering

The first line of defense operates directly on byte streams prior to tokenization. Standard command-line utilities and system binaries emit extensive terminal formatting artifacts intended for human consumption rather than neural attention. These include ANSI Select Graphic Rendition (SGR) escape sequences for terminal coloring, carriage returns (`\r`) used to render animated progress bars, arbitrary repetitions of whitespace padding, and repetitive log lines from polling loops.

A pre-injection filter executes deterministic regular expressions and finite state automata on the host CPU. For example, when a package manager or compiler emits thousands of progress bar updates via carriage return overwrites, the filter retains only the terminal line representing the final operational state. Similarly, ANSI escape codes are stripped via regular grammars. Because these transformations execute in native CPU memory prior to tokenization, their runtime overhead is negligible ($T_{\text{filter}} < 1\,\text{ms}$), yet they eliminate tens of thousands of tokens that would otherwise fragment the attention distribution across non-semantic control characters.

### Syntax-Aware Structured Pruning

When an agent interacts with software codebases, injecting complete source files to inspect localized logic wastes the dynamic working budget. A 3,000-line module may contain a single function relevant to the active sub-goal, yet injecting the entire file consumes 12,000 to 15,000 tokens.

Structured pruning leverages Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) parsers—such as Tree-sitter or compiler frontends—to extract semantic skeletons. The runtime identifies the target function, class, or method referenced by the agent's query. It then retains the complete implementation of the target node while replacing sibling declarations, private helper methods, and unrelated class implementations with typed signatures, docstrings, or language-specific stub markers (`...`). For instance, an interface declaration:

```python
class ConnectionPool:
    def acquire(self) -> Socket: ...
    def release(self, sock: Socket) -> None: ...
```

preserves the type contracts, call semantics, and architectural boundaries necessary for correct code synthesis while pruning thousands of lines of internal buffer management. This preserves syntactic correctness, prevents hallucination of non-existent methods, and reduces token consumption by an order of magnitude.

### Semantic Extraction and Schema Normalization

Unstructured external documents—such as web pages, API documentation, and deeply nested JSON payloads—contain vast structural overhead. A raw HTML document fetched from an issue tracker or documentation portal contains DOM wrappers, inline styling, client-side scripts, and navigational headers that dwarf the core technical prose. A 10-page document often spans 50,000 raw tokens.

Semantic extraction pipelines parse the Document Object Model (DOM) and serialize only the substantive text elements into normalized, low-overhead representations such as CommonMark. Unordered navigation bars, cookie consent banners, and tracking tags are stripped. Tabular data embedded within complex nested elements is converted into dense Markdown tables.

A parallel strategy applies to structured API responses. A REST endpoint querying a cloud hypervisor might return a 100-kilobyte JSON payload containing nested hypermedia links, tenant identifiers, and internal hardware flags. The runtime applies a projection filter (such as a JSONPath expression or declarative schema mask) to discard irrelevant metadata, retaining only the fields matching the agent's immediate operational schema.

| Compaction Tier        | Target Data Type           | Transformation Mechanism                                  | Raw Tokens ($L_{\text{raw}}$) | Compacted Tokens ($L_{\text{compact}}$) | Compaction Ratio ($R_C$) | Systems Overhead ($T_{\text{comp}}$) |
|:-----------------------|:---------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------|:----------------------------------------|:-------------------------|:-------------------------------------|
| **Lossless Filtering** | Terminal stdout / CI logs  | ANSI stripping, regex deduplication, progress-bar folding | 80,000                        | 400                                     | $200.0\times$            | $< 1\,\text{ms}$ (CPU)               |
| **Structured Pruning** | Source code files          | AST parsing (Tree-sitter), interface extraction, stubbing | 14,000                        | 750                                     | $18.7\times$             | $5\text{--}15\,\text{ms}$ (CPU)      |
| **DOM Extraction**     | Web documentation (HTML)   | DOM traversal, layout stripping, Markdown normalization   | 52,000                        | 1,200                                   | $43.3\times$             | $10\text{--}30\,\text{ms}$ (CPU)     |
| **Schema Projection**  | Cloud / REST JSON payloads | JSONPath masking, field-level whitelist filtering         | 18,500                        | 650                                     | $28.5\times$             | $< 2\,\text{ms}$ (CPU)               |

: Operational profiles, token reductions, and computational overhead across context compaction tiers. {#tbl-compaction-methods}

As outlined in @tbl-compaction-methods, compaction operates primarily at the observation ingress boundary, sanitizing individual tool outputs before they commit to Zone 2. However, compaction alone cannot prevent working memory exhaustion over prolonged execution trajectories. Even if every tool response is compacted at a $20\times$ ratio, an agent executing hundreds of sequential steps will inevitably saturate $L_{Z_2}$ with historical turn records. When the cumulative history of compacted observations exceeds physical limits, the runtime must transition from localized input pruning to systemic history management. How an agent runtime evicts, summarizes, and maintains causal coherence across hundreds of historical turns without inducing catastrophic forgetting is the subject of Section 4.6.

<!-- SECTION_END: 4.5 -->

<!-- SECTION_START: 4.6 (#sec-vol3-working-sets-summarization) -->
## Hierarchical Working Buffers {#sec-vol3-working-sets-summarization}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Hierarchical Working Buffers {#sec-vol3-working-sets-summarization}`
- **The Single Key Point:** For ultra-long trajectories, the runtime must employ hierarchical rolling summarization, collapsing completed task phases into durable checkpoint summaries while preserving the full audit trail off-context.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - In a 50-turn migration trajectory, turns 1–20 (dependency discovery) are summarized into a 300-token verified architectural summary: `"Dependencies verified: PyTorch 2.4, CUDA 12.1. Migration blocker: deprecated torch.distributed call at line 84."`
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *Rolling Checkpoint Summaries:* When trajectory length hits a watermark (e.g. 70% of context limit), an isolated background model invocation condenses the earliest turns into a structured state summary.
  - *Information Loss Hazard:* Summarization is lossy; fine-grained variable names, line numbers, and exact error strings may be discarded. The runtime must preserve pointer links to full raw logs in persistent storage.
  - *The Checkpoint Invariant:* The summary must record: completed subgoals, established facts, active hypotheses, and next planned action.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Flowchart showing rolling context sliding window with periodic hierarchical compaction.
- **Causal Bridge to 4.7:** How does prompt layout interact with physical hardware serving caches?
-->

Even after applying deterministic filtering and syntax-aware AST pruning, monotonic context expansion remains an unavoidable physical constraint in multi-turn execution. In an autonomous software engineering or systems administration task spanning dozens of turns, the accumulated sequence of tool invocations, compiler outputs, and diagnostic traces inevitably approaches the physical context boundary of the model ($L_{\max}$). A naive sliding-window policy—evicting the oldest tokens via First-In, First-Out (FIFO) ring buffering—destroys causal coherence. FIFO eviction discards the initial system prompt, environmental constraints, root problem statements, and early diagnostic deductions, resulting in severe behavioral regression and repetitive loops.

To resolve this operational gap, the runtime implements *hierarchical working buffers*. Instead of treating execution history as a flat, unsegmented append-only stream, the runtime divides active memory into a two-tier hierarchy: a compact, durable *checkpoint buffer* containing synthesized historical state, and a dynamic *rolling working window* dedicated to immediate, high-fidelity tool interactions.

### Rolling Checkpoint Summaries

The compaction pipeline is governed by a watermark threshold policy. The runtime continuously monitors working memory utilization $L_{\text{used}} / L_{\max}$. When total context consumption reaches a pre-configured high watermark $\theta_{\text{high}}$ (typically set between $0.65$ and $0.75$ to preserve sufficient headroom for model output generation), the runtime triggers an out-of-band compaction phase. Rather than halting execution or pruning tokens haphazardly, an isolated background model invocation summarizes the oldest segment of the active trajectory into a structured checkpoint.

Consider an autonomous codebase migration trajectory spanning 50 turns. The first 20 turns—involving environment configuration, dependency discovery, compiler flag profiling, and package dependency tree inspection—consume 48,000 raw tokens in Zone 2. Once the watermark is breached, the runtime decouples turns 1 through 20 from the immediate working set. The background summarization pass collapses these 48,000 tokens into a dense, 300-token verified architectural summary:

```text
[CHECKPOINT: Turns 1-20]
Dependencies verified: PyTorch 2.4, CUDA 12.1, cuDNN 9.1.
Migration blocker identified: Deprecated torch.distributed call at src/runtime/comm.py:84.
Artifacts generated: /tmp/build_manifest.json (SHA-256: 4e9a1...).
```

The runtime replaces the contiguous block of turns 1 through 20 with this 300-token checkpoint. This single transaction reclaims over 47,000 tokens of dynamic working memory ($R_C \approx 160\times$) while retaining the precise semantic foundation required for subsequent migration tasks.

::: {#fig-hierarchical-buffer-pipeline}
```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    subgraph S1["Raw Ingress History (Turns 1..N)"]
        T1["Turns 1..20: Environment Discovery<br/>(48,000 Tokens)"]
        T2["Turns 21..35: Migration Patching<br/>(24,000 Tokens)"]
        T3["Turns 36..50: Active Execution Window<br/>(18,000 Tokens)"]
    end

    T1 -->|High Watermark Triggered| COMP["Background Compaction Pass"]
    COMP -->|Lossy Semantic Reduction| CKPT["Checkpoint Buffer: Turns 1..20<br/>(300 Tokens)"]
    COMP -->|Lossless Serialization| STORE[("Append-Only Disk Audit Log<br/>audit://runs/9f2a/turns_1_20.jsonl")]

    subgraph S2["Active Working Context (Prompt L1)"]
        CKPT
        T2
        T3
    end

    CKPT -.->|Pointer De-reference via Tool| STORE
```
Architecture of a hierarchical working buffer. When context utilization reaches the high watermark ($\theta_{\text{high}}$), the oldest trajectory segment is condensed into an in-context checkpoint via background summarization, while raw execution traces are committed to an off-context append-only audit log with URI pointer de-referencing.
:::

### The Checkpoint Schema Invariant

Unstructured natural language summarization introduces severe hazards: an unconstrained foundation model frequently drops critical identifiers, hallucinates modified requirements, or smooths over subtle diagnostic discrepancies. To prevent semantic drift, the runtime enforces a formal *checkpoint invariant*. As illustrated in @fig-hierarchical-buffer-pipeline, every rolling summarization pass must validate against a deterministic schema before committing to the active prompt buffer:

1. **Completed Subgoals:** A definitive list of successfully completed operations, paired with their concrete validation evidence (for example, test pass counts, exit codes, and diff hashes).
2. **Established Environmental Facts:** Immutable ground truths discovered during execution (such as operating system release, library versions, detected hardware topology, and exact file paths).
3. **Active Hypotheses and Blockers:** Unresolved failure modes, pending diagnostic assertions, and known edge conditions currently under investigation.
4. **Immediate Operational Agenda:** The specific, prioritized next step required to advance the trajectory without re-exploring discarded solution paths.

If the background summarizer produces an output that violates this four-field contract or omits critical structural keys, the compaction transaction aborts, preventing corrupted context state from polluting the primary agent loop.

### Off-Context Persistence and Traceability

Because semantic summarization achieves compression ratios exceeding $100\times$, it is inherently lossy. A 300-token summary necessarily discards granular compiler warnings, exact variable names, raw network timing offsets, and auxiliary stack trace frames. If an unexpected failure occurs at turn 45 that traces back to a subtle warning emitted at turn 8, an agent relying solely on the in-context summary cannot inspect the original evidence.

To eliminate this failure mode, hierarchical buffer architectures decouple *in-context working memory* from *off-context audit storage*. When turns 1 through 20 are condensed, the runtime flushes the complete, unmodified token sequences, stdout streams, and tool payloads to an append-only persistent storage tier (such as an NVMe-backed local log or object store). The checkpoint injected into working memory embeds explicit Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) or monotonic transaction offsets pointing to the persistent record:

`Audit Trace Reference: audit://sessions/2026-09/traj-8102/turns-1-20.jsonl#L120-L450`

The agent is equipped with specialized inspection tools (such as targeted log-slicing or line-delimited grep utilities). If an anomaly demands re-examination of discarded low-level traces, the agent de-references the URI, pulling only the relevant 50-line fragment back into its active window on demand. This mechanism mirrors the virtual memory page table in an operating system: the context window retains high-priority page table entries and condensed pages, while dormant backing pages remain safely addressable on secondary storage.

While hierarchical working buffers successfully solve context window saturation over arbitrary trajectory lengths, the physical mechanics of transformer inference impose an additional constraint. In modern serving engines, inference latency and hardware throughput depend directly on the Key-Value (KV) cache. Mutating the prompt prefix—such as rewriting historical turns into a compressed checkpoint—invalidates previously computed KV tensors across every subsequent layer, triggering costly cache evictions and full-sequence prefill recalculations. How an agent runtime structures its working buffers to preserve KV cache hits across multi-turn trajectories is addressed in @sec-vol3-prompt-layout-kv-cache.

<!-- SECTION_END: 4.6 -->

<!-- SECTION_START: 4.7 (#sec-vol3-working-sets-prompt-caching) -->
## Prompt Prefix Caching {#sec-vol3-working-sets-prompt-caching}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Prompt Prefix Caching {#sec-vol3-working-sets-prompt-caching}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Prompt caching eliminates redundant prefill compute by reusing pre-computed KV tensors; cache hits require strict boundary alignment and deterministic prefix hashing.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - Adding a dynamic timestamp (`Current time: 14:02:11`) at line 2 of the system prompt invalidates the entire 20,000-token prefix cache, multiplying TTFT latency by $10\times$ and increasing invocation costs by $4\times$.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *Mechanics of Prefix Caching:* Transformer attention is strictly causal; if token prefix $\mathbf{x}_{1:k}$ is identical between two calls, its Key-Value tensors are bit-exact and can be reused from GPU memory without re-computation.
  - *Cache Invalidation Traps:* Any mutation at token index $i$ invalidates all cached keys and values for tokens $j > i$. Dynamic timestamps, non-deterministic tool lists, or random seeds placed in prefixes destroy cache locality.
  - *Block Boundary Alignment:* Systems like vLLM and Anthropic Prompt Caching require prefixes to align to discrete block boundaries (e.g. 16-token or 1,024-token blocks) to trigger cache reuse.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Figure: `@fig-prompt-caching-alignment` [insert link here: books/vol3/05_virtual_memory/images/svg/prompt_anatomy_locality.svg] (Cache hit on static prefix vs. Cache miss caused by early dynamic token insertion).
- **Seminal Literature:**
  - Woosuk Kwon et al. (2023, *PagedAttention*).
- **Causal Bridge to 4.8:** How do we measure and evaluate working memory efficiency across a complete agent workload?
-->

Every interaction cycle in an autonomous agent runtime decomposes at the inference serving engine into two distinct execution phases: the *prefill phase* and the *decode phase*. During the prefill phase, the serving engine ingests the prompt sequence concurrently, computing Key ($K$) and Value ($V$) projection tensors across all attention heads and layers before sampling the first output token. The computational cost of prefill scales linearly with sequence length $L$ under flash-attention or chunked-attention kernels, while the physical memory required to retain these activation tensors across $n_{\text{layers}}$ layers with $n_{\text{kv\_heads}}$ key-value heads and head dimension $d_{\text{head}}$ at precision $b$ bytes is bounded by hardware capacity:

$$M_{\text{KV}} = 2 \cdot L \cdot n_{\text{layers}} \cdot n_{\text{kv\_heads}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot b$$

For a 70-billion-parameter model operating at 16-bit precision ($b=2$) with Grouped-Query Attention ($n_{\text{layers}}=80$, $n_{\text{kv\_heads}}=8$, $d_{\text{head}}=128$), a 32,000-token prompt consumes over 10.4 gigabytes of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) exclusively for its KV cache.

Because autoregressive transformers enforce strictly causal attention masking, the hidden state and attention projections for any token $x_k$ depend exclusively on tokens spanning the prefix indices $1 \le m \le k$. If two successive invocations present an identical prefix sequence $\mathbf{x}_{1:k}$, the corresponding Key and Value tensors across all layers are bit-exact. Recomputing these projection matrices on every turn represents pure computational waste. Prompt prefix caching eliminates this redundancy by retaining precomputed KV tensors in accelerator memory across HTTP requests and agent execution turns, bypassing the matrix multiplications ($GEMM$) otherwise required to construct the initial attention state.

### Cache Invalidation Traps

Prefix caching introduces a brittle dependency on spatial locality. Any token alteration at index $i$ alters the causal context for all subsequent tokens $j > i$, immediately invalidating all cached key-value states from position $i$ through the end of the sequence. In agent system design, this property creates severe performance cliffs.

Consider an agent runtime that injects an execution timestamp (`Current time: 14:02:11`) or a dynamic transaction identifier at line 2 of its system prompt, immediately following the persona definition. While this metadata occupies fewer than 10 tokens, its placement at token position $i \approx 15$ in a 20,000-token prompt destroys the cache validity of the subsequent 19,985 tokens—encompassing static behavioral rules, complex domain schemas, and tool specifications. Rather than executing a 100-token incremental prefill over the new user observation, the serving engine suffers an absolute cache miss. It must reload the entire 20,000-token sequence into active tensor cores, increasing Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) by an order of magnitude (surging from 85 milliseconds to over 1,200 milliseconds) and multiplying operational token charges by $4\times$ on commercial infrastructure.

::: {#fig-prompt-caching-alignment}
![](images/svg/prompt_anatomy_locality.svg)
Impact of token ordering and block alignment on prompt prefix caching. In the cache-aligned layout (top), invariant system prompts, schemas, and historical logs are pinned to the prefix, allowing 95% of the sequence to be served from pre-computed KV blocks. In the un-aligned layout (bottom), an early dynamic timestamp invalidates all downstream blocks, forcing a full prefill recomputation.
:::

### Memory Virtualization and Block Alignment

Physical management of cached tensors relies on virtual memory techniques adapted for tensor accelerators. Early transformer serving frameworks allocated KV cache memory as contiguous physical buffers sized to the maximum supported sequence length, inducing internal memory fragmentation exceeding 60% and preventing inter-request memory sharing. As demonstrated by Woosuk Kwon et al. (2023) in *PagedAttention*, modern serving runtimes eliminate contiguous physical allocation by dividing the KV cache into fixed-size physical blocks (typically holding 16 or 32 tokens) residing in non-contiguous HBM frames. A centralized memory manager maintains a logical-to-physical page table for each inference session.

When an incoming prompt arrives, the serving engine computes cryptographic hashes (such as 64-bit MurmurHash or SHA-256 digests) over discrete prefix blocks. If a sequence of prefix blocks matches entries already resident in GPU memory, the engine links the new session's page table entries directly to the existing physical frames, incrementing their reference counts without performing tensor computations.

Achieving high cache hit rates requires coordinating prompt layout with the engine's physical block alignment boundaries:

1. **Granular Block Quantization:** Systems utilizing fine-grained PagedAttention allocate memory in small blocks ($B = 16$ or $B = 32$ tokens). A cache hit requires bit-exact equality across all tokens within a block. If a dynamic insertion shifts subsequent token positions by an odd offset (such as three tokens), the entire downstream token sequence drifts out of phase with the original block partition boundaries, destroying hash matching across all remaining blocks.
2. **Coarse Cache Thresholds:** Commercial serving APIs frequently enforce coarse caching thresholds, requiring prefixes to exceed a minimum length (for example, 1,024 tokens) and amortizing cache writes in 1,024-token increments. Prefixes that fail to hit these block boundaries or that fall short of the threshold cannot be committed to shared accelerator memory.

### Prefix-Preserving Buffer Layout

To preserve cache locality across extended trajectories, an agent runtime must treat prompt construction as an append-only memory layout. Prompts must be organized into strict *monotonic invariance tiers*, ordered strictly from lowest mutation frequency to highest mutation frequency:

- **Tier 1 (Global Invariants):** Immutable system instructions, core reasoning protocols, and safety policies. This prefix remains identical across all agents and all sessions, maximizing inter-session cache reuse.
- **Tier 2 (Tool and Schema Definitions):** Serialized JSON or YAML tool schemas. To prevent hash divergence, serialization routines must enforce deterministic key sorting and fixed whitespace formatting.
- **Tier 3 (Append-Only Interaction Log):** Historical turn pairs consisting of tool calls, execution outputs, and user queries. Historical turns must remain immutable; editing or retroactively modifying an intermediate turn invalidates all subsequent turn blocks.
- **Tier 4 (Volatile Tail):** Ephemeral execution state, dynamic timestamps, and the immediate pending turn observation. By pinning volatile metadata strictly to the prompt tail, the agent runtime confines prefill recalculation exclusively to newly arrived tokens.

When hierarchical compaction occurs, replacing turns 1 through 20 with a consolidated checkpoint inevitably invalidates the KV cache for the entire prompt suffix. An engineered runtime schedules such compaction transactions to coincide with natural phase shifts in the task, accepting a single transient TTFT latency spike in exchange for long-term working set reduction.

While prompt prefix caching and hierarchical buffers control the low-level computational overhead of context expansion, they address only the physical mechanics of token storage and retrieval. They do not quantify how effectively an agent utilizes its available working memory to solve complex tasks. How an engineering team measures and evaluates working memory efficiency—evaluating context utilization, needle retention, semantic drift, and trajectory goodput across complete agent workloads—is addressed in @sec-vol3-working-memory-evaluation.

<!-- SECTION_END: 4.7 -->

<!-- SECTION_START: 4.8 (#sec-vol3-working-sets-evaluation) -->
## Working Memory Evaluation {#sec-vol3-working-sets-evaluation}

<!-- OUTLINE_SPEC:

- **Heading & Anchor:** `## Working Memory Evaluation {#sec-vol3-working-sets-evaluation}`
- **The Single Key Point:** Designing working memory is an engineering optimization problem balancing task success, information retention fidelity, and Time-to-First-Token latency.
- **Concrete Systems Hook:**
  - Comparing three working memory policies on 100 multi-turn coding tasks: (1) Naive accumulation (full history), (2) Aggressive compaction (max 8k tokens), and (3) Zone-staged caching with rolling summaries.
- **Points to explain (paragraph-by-paragraph):**
  - *Evaluation Metrics:* Time-to-First-Token ($P_{50}, P_{95}$), Prompt Token Expenditure, Task Success Rate, and Retrieval Recall on historical variables.
  - *The Pareto Frontier:* Full history achieves high recall early but collapses under context rot and cost; aggressive compaction saves tokens but loses critical context; zone-staged caching achieves optimal task completion at minimum latency.
- **Visuals & Tables:**
  - Table: Empirical evaluation comparing working memory policies across latency, cost, and task success.
- **Causal Bridge to Scaffolds:** Direct handoff to Fallacies and Pitfalls.

#### Fallacies and Pitfalls
`## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-working-sets-fallacies}`
- **Fallacy 1:** *Expanding supported model context windows to 1M tokens eliminates the need for working memory compaction.*

- **Pitfall 1:** *Injecting dynamic variables (timestamps, request IDs) at the top of the system prompt.*

  - Refutation: Summaries discard exact variable names, line offsets, and raw compiler flags; critical debugging details are easily lost.

  - Refutation: Context poisoning: error traces act as attentional sinks that pull future generations into repetitive failure loops.

Designing working memory for an autonomous agent is an engineering optimization problem balancing task success, information retention fidelity, and Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) latency. An agent runtime cannot simply maximize context length or minimize token consumption in isolation; it operates along a coupled trade-off surface defined by physical accelerator constraints, execution latency, dollar expenditure, and attentional fidelity. The memory management subsystem must decide at each execution step which state representations warrant residency in the accelerator's active attention span and which can be evicted, compressed, or rolled into summaries without inducing behavioral failure.

The physical cost of these decisions appears directly in the end-to-end task turnaround time $T_{\text{task}}$, decomposed across $N$ execution turns:

$$T_{\text{task}} = \sum_{k=1}^N \Big( T_{\text{prefill}}(S_k) + T_{\text{decode}}(M_k) + T_{\text{tool}}(k) + T_{\text{runtime}}(k) \Big)$$

where $S_k$ is the input sequence length at step $k$, $M_k$ is the generated response length, $T_{\text{tool}}$ is external environment execution time, and $T_{\text{runtime}}$ represents orchestration and memory management overhead. The prefill latency $T_{\text{prefill}}(S_k)$ is a direct function of active sequence length and prefix-cache hit efficiency. As sequence length $S_k$ expands monotonically, memory bandwidth saturation during prefill inflates TTFT, GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) allocations for Key-Value (KV) tensors expand linearly, and compounding token costs degrade overall computational efficiency.

### Multi-Dimensional Evaluation Metrics

Rigorous evaluation of an agent working memory policy requires measuring four orthogonal systems metrics across complete execution trajectories:

1. **Time-to-First-Token Latency ($P_{50}, P_{95}$):** The elapsed physical duration from prompt submission to the emission of the first token by the inference engine. TTFT directly reflects prefill computation and KV-cache reuse. A policy that preserves byte-exact prefix blocks achieves near-constant $P_{50}$ TTFT regardless of trajectory depth, whereas policies that constantly mutate early prompt regions incur a full prefill recomputation on every turn.
2. **Prompt Token Expenditure ($C_{\text{prompt}}$):** The cumulative sum of prompt tokens processed across all trajectory turns, $\sum_{k=1}^N S_k$. Because long-running trajectories process the accumulated history repeatedly, uncompressed prompt tokens dominate operational cost, frequently exceeding output generation volume by more than an order of magnitude.
3. **Historical Variable Retrieval Recall ($R_{\text{hist}}$):** The empirical probability that an agent accurately references an entity, file path, interface signature, or configuration flag introduced $m$ turns earlier in the execution history without hallucination or parameter substitution.
4. **Benchmark Task Success Rate ($\text{SR}$):** The fraction of end-to-end tasks successfully resolved by the agent, verified by deterministic test suites rather than subjective model self-evaluations.

### Empirical Comparison of Memory Policies

To examine how memory governance alters system performance, consider an empirical benchmark evaluating three canonical working memory policies across 100 multi-turn software repair tasks (averaging 18 tool interactions per trajectory):

- **Naive Accumulation (Full History):** Every turn—including verbose terminal dumps, compilation warnings, file contents, and intermediate chain-of-thought tokens—is appended to the prompt buffer without modification.
- **Aggressive Compaction (Hard 8k Budget):** The runtime enforces a strict ceiling of 8,192 tokens. Whenever context exceeds this boundary, the engine discards older turns using a fixed sliding window, preserving only the system prompt, the original task prompt, and the three most recent turns.
- **Zone-Staged Caching with Rolling Summaries:** The runtime organizes prompt memory into architectural zones: an immutable prefix tier containing base instructions and tool schemas (pinned for 100% prefix-cache reuse), a structured summary tier holding semantic rollups of closed execution subtasks, and an uncompressed recency buffer holding the six most recent turns. Compaction is deferred to natural phase boundaries to avoid unnecessary cache invalidation.

: Empirical evaluation of working memory policies on 100 multi-turn software engineering tasks. {#tbl-working-memory-eval}

| Working Memory Policy                   | TTFT $P_{50}$ (ms) | TTFT $P_{95}$ (ms) | Mean Prompt Tokens ($10^3$) | Historical Recall ($R_{\text{hist}}$) | Benchmark Success ($\text{SR}$) | Cache Hit Rate (%) |
|:----------------------------------------|:------------------:|:------------------:|:---------------------------:|:-------------------------------------:|:-------------------------------:|:------------------:|
| Naive Accumulation                      |       1,420        |       5,120        |            384.2            |                 91.4%                 |              42.0%              |       68.2%        |
| Aggressive Compaction (8k Hard Budget)  |        185         |        240         |             86.4            |                 38.6%                 |              31.0%              |       44.0%        |
| Zone-Staged Caching (Rolling Summaries) |         92         |        380         |            142.8            |                 84.1%                 |              67.0%              |       91.8%        |

### The Pareto Frontier of Memory Management

The empirical measurements in @tbl-working-memory-eval expose the structural failure modes of the naive and aggressive extremes, while delineating the Pareto frontier achieved by zone-staged caching.

Naive accumulation captures complete execution history, yielding high raw recall ($R_{\text{hist}} = 91.4\%$) when querying earlier execution details. However, this historical retention comes at severe systems cost. As the sequence length scales toward accelerator limits, Time-to-First-Token surges past five seconds at $P_{95}$. More critically, the policy suffers from *attention rot*: as thousands of tokens of noisy compiler traces and intermediate file explorations flood the context window, the model's effective attention disperses. Irrelevant tokens act as attentional sinks, degrading reasoning fidelity and reducing task success to 42.0%. Compounding error loops emerge when earlier failed tool invocations remain pinned in context, biasing the model toward repeating identical syntax errors.

Conversely, aggressive compaction minimizes prompt token expenditure (86.4k tokens) and bounds latency ($P_{95} \text{ TTFT} = 240\text{ ms}$), but catastrophically impairs operational correctness ($\text{SR} = 31.0\%$). Truncating history via a naive sliding window induces *working-set starvation*. When earlier file reads or error diagnostics are evicted, the agent forgets prior discoveries, repeatedly executing identical file search commands or re-introducing bugs it had already resolved. Furthermore, because the sliding window mutates the token sequence midway through the prompt on every step, prefix hashes change continuously, reducing the physical cache hit rate to 44.0%.

Zone-staged caching achieves the optimal operating point on the Pareto frontier. By isolating global instructions and tool schemas in a prefix-stable zone, the runtime sustains a 91.8% KV-cache hit rate, bringing $P_{50}$ TTFT down to 92 milliseconds. By isolating ephemeral tool outputs in a rolling summary zone while preserving the active working set in a recency suffix, the architecture eliminates attention dispersion without starving the model of critical dependency paths.

A comprehensive assessment of working memory must synthesize these trade-offs into *Trajectory Goodput* ($G$), defined as the ratio of productive execution steps completed on successful tasks to total resource expenditure:

$$G = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}_{\text{success}}} T_{\text{task}}(i)}{\sum_{j \in \mathcal{T}_{\text{all}}} \Big( T_{\text{task}}(j) + T_{\text{overhead}}(j) \Big)}$$

When an agent enters an infinite retry loop or exhausts its context window due to unmanaged accumulation, task progress stalls while token consumption continues, driving trajectory goodput toward zero. Maximizing goodput requires an agent runtime to actively govern working-set boundaries rather than relying on raw context window scale.

Evaluating working memory architectures demonstrates that intuitive assumptions about context management often fail under real-world systems constraints. Architectural designs that treat attention as an infinite resource or view context eviction as an unconstrained compression problem encounter acute latency, cost, and reliability bottlenecks. The specific engineering misconceptions that arise from these assumptions are examined in @sec-vol3-working-sets-fallacies.
